title: Conflict, Peace and Religious Freedom
bigQuestion: When have religious communities been part of war, when have they been part of making peace, and how can a society protect the freedom of every faith and of those with none?

story.title: The Front Row at Selma
story.kicker: In March 1965 clergy of many faiths answered a call to Selma, Alabama, and walked beside the marchers who were demanding the right to vote.
paragraphs: On Sunday, March 7, 1965, about six hundred people set out from a church in Selma, Alabama, to march to the state capital in Montgomery. They were demanding the right to vote, which Black citizens in the county had been denied for generations. At the Edmund Pettus Bridge, state troopers and a sheriff's posse attacked them with clubs and tear gas. Television cameras filmed it, and the day became known as Bloody Sunday. Within hours, Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist minister, sent telegrams asking clergy across the country to come to Selma.

Hundreds came: ministers, priests, nuns and rabbis, many of them white and from the North. On March 9 one of them, James Reeb, a Unitarian minister from Boston, was beaten by men on a Selma street. He died two days later. At a memorial service in Selma on March 15, Archbishop Iakovos, the head of the Greek Orthodox Church in North and South America, stood beside King in his black robes and tall hat. Photographs of the two men together, an Orthodox archbishop and a Black Baptist preacher, appeared in newspapers across the country.

On March 21, protected this time by federal troops, the march to Montgomery began. In the front row, wearing a flower lei that a group from Hawaii had given the leaders, walked Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel. He was a scholar of the Hebrew prophets who had fled Europe just before the Holocaust and reached the United States in 1940, and he had written that the prophets cared most about the suffering of ordinary people. Afterward he wrote that as he marched he felt as if his legs were praying. Beside him walked King, and beside King the diplomat Ralph Bunche.

The march reached Montgomery on March 25, with a crowd of about twenty-five thousand. That August, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act. Religion had been on both sides of the struggle. Many white churches in the South had defended segregation, and many segregationists were churchgoers. Yet the movement itself was organized in churches, sang hymns and spirituals, and drew its language from the Exodus and the prophets. This chapter asks how the same traditions can be part of both conflict and peace.
story.think: Heschel said his legs were praying. What did he mean, and why might a rabbi, an Orthodox archbishop and a Baptist minister each see marching for voting rights as part of their own faith?

lessons.title: The Crusades
lessons.mainIdea: The Crusades of 1095 to 1291 were wars that Latin Christians fought as religious acts of penance, and they are remembered very differently by Christians, Muslims and Jews.
reading: In November 1095, at a church council in Clermont, France, Pope Urban II called on the knights of Western Europe to march east. The Byzantine emperor had asked for help against the Seljuk Turks, and Jerusalem had been under Muslim rule since the 600s. Urban promised that those who went would receive an *indulgence*, the removal of the penance owed for their sins. Crowds are said to have answered with the cry God wills it. The wars that followed are called the *Crusades*, from the cross that fighters sewed on their clothing. To the men who took the vow, the journey was both a war and a *pilgrimage*, a sacred journey to a holy place.

The First Crusade captured Jerusalem in July 1099, and the crusaders killed many of the city's Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. Even before they left Europe, crusading bands had attacked Jewish communities in the Rhineland in 1096, in Speyer, Worms and Mainz, and Jewish memory still mourns those towns. In 1187 the Muslim ruler Saladin, Salah al-Din in Arabic, retook Jerusalem after defeating a crusader army at Hattin. Muslim and Christian chroniclers alike noted that he allowed most residents to ransom themselves rather than be killed. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade turned aside and sacked Constantinople, a Christian city, deepening the split between Catholic and Orthodox Christians. The last crusader stronghold on the coast, Acre, fell in 1291.

Historians describe mixed motives: sincere devotion, the hope of forgiveness, family honor, land and plunder. Arab writers of the time called the invaders al-Ifranj, the Franks, and often treated them as one more foreign army. In the modern era the word crusade has been used for political purposes, and many Muslims hear it as a symbol of Western attack. Churches have also looked back. In 2001 Pope John Paul II expressed sorrow to the Orthodox Church for the sack of Constantinople. The Crusades show a pattern historians see again and again: religious ideas gave war a purpose and a promise, while politics and power shaped how it was fought.

words.d: wars fought by Latin Christians between 1095 and 1291, above all for control of Jerusalem and the Holy Land
in Catholic teaching, a removal of the penance owed for sins that have been forgiven; promised to crusaders
a journey to a holy place undertaken as a religious act
Salah al-Din, the Muslim ruler of Egypt and Syria who retook Jerusalem from the crusaders in 1187

lessons.title: Wars of Religion in Europe
lessons.mainIdea: After the Reformation, Catholic and Protestant rulers fought for more than a century, and the exhausting Thirty Years' War helped push Europe toward toleration.
reading: After Martin Luther challenged the Catholic Church in 1517, Western Christianity split into Catholic and Protestant churches, and each ruler's choice became a political question. In the Holy Roman Empire, the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 settled the matter with a rule later summed up in a Latin phrase, *cuius regio, eius religio*: whose realm, his religion. Each prince chose Lutheran or Catholic, and his subjects had to follow or move away. Calvinists and other groups were left out. In France, Catholics and Protestant Huguenots fought eight civil wars, and in the Saint Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572 Catholic mobs killed thousands of Huguenots. The Edict of Nantes in 1598 finally gave Huguenots limited rights.

In 1618 Protestant nobles in Prague threw two Catholic imperial officials out of a castle window. Both survived, but the event, called the Defenestration of Prague, set off the *Thirty Years' War*. It spread across the German lands and drew in Denmark, Sweden, Spain and France. Armies lived off the land, and hunger and disease followed them. Estimates vary, but many regions lost a fifth or more of their people. The war was never only about religion. Catholic France, ruled in practice by a cardinal, paid Protestant Sweden to fight the Catholic Habsburg emperor, because France feared Habsburg power more than it cared about the faith of its allies.

The *Peace of Westphalia* in 1648 ended the war. It recognized Calvinists alongside Lutherans and Catholics and allowed some private worship for religious minorities. Many historians see it as a step toward a Europe of sovereign states that did not go to war over doctrine. The long bloodshed also moved thinkers to argue for *toleration*, the acceptance of beliefs one does not share. In 1689 the English philosopher John Locke, a Protestant Christian, wrote A Letter Concerning Toleration. He argued that belief cannot be forced, so governments should protect lives and property and leave the care of souls to churches. Those arguments crossed the Atlantic and shaped the American founders.

words.d: Latin for whose realm, his religion; the 1555 rule that a prince chose the religion of his lands
French Protestants in the Calvinist tradition, who fought Catholic forces in the French Wars of Religion
the war of 1618 to 1648 in the German lands, begun between Catholics and Protestants and widened into a European power struggle
the treaties of 1648 that ended the Thirty Years' War and recognized Calvinists, Lutherans and Catholics
accepting that others hold beliefs and practices one does not share, without punishing them for it

look.title: Locke on Belief and Force
look.text: Locke argued that true religion lies in the inward persuasion of the mind, and that no one can be made to believe something by force. Laws and penalties can make people pretend, but not believe. So the care of souls does not belong to the government. The ruler's task is to protect life, liberty and property, and churches should be free societies that people join by choice.
look.cite: John Locke, A Letter Concerning Toleration, 1689 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: How does Locke's argument respond to the rule of whose realm, his religion? Which events in this lesson might have convinced readers that he was right?

check.q: What did the rule cuius regio, eius religio mean after 1555?
choices: Every person chose his or her own church
The pope chose the religion of each realm
Only Calvinists could rule in the empire
Each prince chose Lutheran or Catholic for his lands, and subjects had to follow or leave
check.why: Under the Peace of Augsburg, whose realm, his religion meant the ruler decided, and Calvinists were left out.

check.q: Why do historians say the Thirty Years' War was not only about religion?
choices: Because it was fought only by Protestants
Because Catholic France paid Protestant Sweden to fight the Catholic Habsburg emperor
Because it ended before any battles took place
Because the pope refused to take a side
check.why: France allied with Protestant Sweden out of fear of Habsburg power, which shows politics shaping the war.

check.q: What did John Locke argue in A Letter Concerning Toleration?
choices: That belief cannot be forced, so government should leave the care of souls to churches
That every nation should have one official church
That only Protestants should hold office
That religious wars were a duty of princes
check.why: Locke held that force can make people pretend but not believe, so the state should protect life and property and leave faith to churches.

lessons.title: The Partition of India
lessons.mainIdea: In 1947 British India was divided into India and Pakistan along religious lines, and the partition brought mass migration and killing among Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs.
reading: At midnight on August 14 and 15, 1947, British rule in South Asia ended and two countries were born: India, with a Hindu majority, and Pakistan, created as a homeland for Muslims. The Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, had argued that Muslims would be a permanent minority in a united India. The Indian National Congress, led by Jawaharlal Nehru and Mohandas Gandhi, had wanted one country for people of all faiths. A British lawyer who had never been to India drew the new border in a few weeks. It split the provinces of *Punjab* in the west and Bengal in the east, where Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs had lived in the same villages for centuries.

The *Partition* set off one of the largest migrations in history. Estimates vary, but roughly fifteen million people crossed the new borders, Muslims moving to Pakistan and Hindus and Sikhs moving to India. Mobs on every side attacked trains, villages and refugee columns. Estimates of the dead range from several hundred thousand to two million, and tens of thousands of women were abducted. Sikhs lost much of their homeland in western Punjab, including Nankana Sahib, the birthplace of Guru Nanak, which now lies in Pakistan. Families on both sides still tell stories of neighbors who hid them and neighbors who turned on them.

Gandhi spent the days of independence in Calcutta, living in a Muslim neighborhood to calm the violence. In September 1947, and again in Delhi in January 1948, he fasted until leaders promised to stop the killing. On January 30, 1948, he was shot dead by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for being too generous to Muslims. Scholars of Partition stress that religion marked the communities, but fear, politics and the speed of the British exit turned neighbors into enemies. In 2019 India and Pakistan opened the Kartarpur Corridor, which lets Indian Sikh pilgrims cross into Pakistan without a visa to visit the gurdwara where Guru Nanak spent his last years.

words.d: the division of British India in 1947 into India and Pakistan, largely along religious lines
a region of northwest South Asia, homeland of the Sikhs, split between India and Pakistan in 1947
the political party, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, that called for a separate Muslim homeland in Pakistan
a person forced to flee home because of war, persecution or disaster

look.title: Two Neighbors, One Village
look.text: In a village in Punjab in 1946, a Sikh farmer and a Muslim farmer share a well and attend each other's weddings. In August 1947 the new border runs a few miles away. Rumors arrive of trains full of the dead. One family must leave. The other must decide whether to hide its neighbors or stay silent. Oral histories collected decades later record both choices, often in the same village.
look.prompt: What forces other than religious belief were pushing on these two families in August 1947? Why do historians of Partition collect oral histories from ordinary people rather than relying only on leaders' speeches?

choices: It argued that Muslims would be a permanent minority in a united India
It wanted to join the British Empire permanently
It hoped to create a Sikh homeland
It opposed independence from Britain
check.why: Under Jinnah, the Muslim League argued that Muslims needed their own homeland, which became Pakistan.

check.q: Why was Partition especially painful for Sikhs?
choices: Sikhs were forbidden to cross the border
Sikhs were given all of Bengal

The Sikh Gurus had predicted the division
check.why: The line cut through Punjab, and Guru Nanak's birthplace at Nankana Sahib ended up in Pakistan.

check.q: How did Gandhi respond to the violence of Partition?

He lived in a Muslim neighborhood in Calcutta and fasted to stop the killing

check.why: Gandhi stayed in a Muslim area of Calcutta and fasted there and in Delhi until leaders pledged to end the violence.

lessons.title: Northern Ireland and the Question of Cause
lessons.mainIdea: In Northern Ireland religion marked two communities, but scholars describe the Troubles mainly as a conflict over national identity, rights and power.
reading: In the early 1600s the English crown settled Protestant colonists from Scotland and England on land taken from Catholic Irish in the northern province of Ulster. When most of Ireland won independence in 1921, six counties of Ulster stayed in the United Kingdom as Northern Ireland, with a Protestant majority. Many Catholics there faced discrimination in jobs, housing and voting. In the late 1960s a civil rights movement marched for equal treatment, and violence followed. The period from about 1968 to 1998 is called the *Troubles*. More than 3,500 people were killed, many by armed groups on both sides and some by British soldiers, as on Bloody Sunday in Derry in January 1972.

The two sides are often called Protestant and Catholic, but most people there use political names. *Unionists*, mostly Protestant, wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom. *Nationalists*, mostly Catholic, wanted it to join the Republic of Ireland. Few fighters argued about doctrine, such as the Mass or the authority of the pope. Scholars therefore describe religion here as an identity marker: it told people which community they belonged to, which school they attended and which neighborhood was safe. The same pattern appears in many conflicts where faith and nationality overlap.

Religious people also worked for peace. In 1965 a Presbyterian minister, Ray Davey, founded the Corrymeela Community, where Catholics and Protestants met for reconciliation. A Catholic priest, Father Alec Reid of Clonard Monastery in Belfast, carried secret messages between political leaders for years. The Good Friday Agreement, signed on April 10, 1998, created a shared government and was approved by voters in both parts of Ireland. For students of religion the case raises a lasting question: when a conflict is labeled religious, what exactly is religion doing in it?

words.d: the period of violent conflict in Northern Ireland from about 1968 to 1998
in Northern Ireland, people, usually Protestant, who want to remain part of the United Kingdom
in Northern Ireland, people, usually Catholic, who want to join the Republic of Ireland
a feature, such as religion or language, that shows which group a person belongs to
restoring a relationship after conflict, through meeting, truth-telling and forgiveness

look.title: Is It About Religion?

Second: it was a national conflict between people who saw themselves as British and people who saw themselves as Irish. Third: it was a struggle over civil rights, jobs and housing, in which religion marked who got what. Each explanation can point to real evidence.
look.prompt: Using the reading, which explanation do most scholars favor, and what evidence would you use to test each one? Could all three be partly true?

check.why: Unionists, mostly Protestant, wanted to stay in the United Kingdom; nationalists wanted to join Ireland.

check.q: Why do scholars call religion an identity marker in the Troubles?
choices: Because fighters argued mostly about the Mass and the pope
Because religion told people which community, school and neighborhood they belonged to
Because neither side had any religious members
Because the churches ran the armed groups
check.why: Few people fought over doctrine; religion signaled belonging in a conflict over nationality and rights.

check.q: What role did Father Alec Reid play in Northern Ireland?

He signed the Good Friday Agreement as prime minister
He led unionist marches
He carried secret messages between political leaders to help start peace talks
check.why: The Catholic priest at Clonard Monastery quietly passed messages between leaders; Ray Davey founded Corrymeela.

lessons.title: Gandhi and Truth-Force
lessons.mainIdea: Gandhi built a method of nonviolent resistance, satyagraha, from Hindu and Jain ideas of ahimsa, the Bhagavad Gita and the Sermon on the Mount.
reading: In March 1930 Mohandas Gandhi, sixty years old, set out on foot from his ashram near Ahmedabad with about eighty followers. British law made it a crime for Indians to make their own salt, and salt was taxed. Over twenty-four days the group walked about 240 miles to the sea at Dandi, and thousands joined along the way. On April 6 Gandhi picked up a lump of natural salt from the shore and broke the law. Across India, people made salt and filled the jails. The *Salt March* made his method visible to the world.

Gandhi called the method *satyagraha*, a word he coined from the Sanskrit for truth and holding firmly: truth-force. It meant resisting injustice openly, accepting punishment without striking back, and trying to win over the opponent rather than defeat him. Its root was *ahimsa*, nonharm, a central teaching of Jainism that runs through Hinduism and Buddhism as well. Gandhi grew up in Gujarat, where Jain influence was strong. He read the Bhagavad Gita daily and took from it the ideal of acting for duty without attachment to reward. He also said the Sermon on the Mount went straight to his heart, and he corresponded with the Russian writer Leo Tolstoy, whose books on that sermon had moved him.

Gandhi developed satyagraha in South Africa, where he lived from 1893 to 1914, before leading the Indian independence movement. Not every Indian agreed with him. Some wanted armed revolt, some thought his religious language excluded Muslims or lower castes, and B. R. Ambedkar, the leader of the Dalits, opposed him on caste. India won independence in 1947. Gandhi's method crossed religious lines. A Pashtun Muslim, Abdul Ghaffar Khan, raised a nonviolent army in the northwest, and a generation later Martin Luther King Jr. traveled to India in 1959 to learn from Gandhi's legacy.

words.d: truth-force; Gandhi's method of open, nonviolent resistance to injustice, accepting punishment without retaliation
nonharm or nonviolence toward all living beings; central to Jainism and important in Hinduism and Buddhism
Gandhi's 240-mile walk to the sea in 1930 to break the British salt law in protest
a member of the communities once treated as outside the Hindu caste order and called untouchable

lessons.title: King and the Beloved Community
lessons.mainIdea: Martin Luther King Jr. joined the Bible's prophets and the Sermon on the Mount with Gandhi's method to lead a nonviolent movement for civil rights.
reading: In December 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, and Black residents began a boycott of the city buses that lasted more than a year. They chose as their leader a twenty-six-year-old Baptist pastor, Martin Luther King Jr. The boycott was organized in churches, and its mass meetings mixed hymns, prayer and planning. King told the crowds that they would resist with love. In 1956 the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The *civil rights movement* that followed drew much of its strength and language from Black churches.

King described a goal he called the *beloved community*, a society where former enemies are reconciled and every person's dignity is honored. He drew it from the Hebrew prophets, especially Amos's call to let justice roll down like waters, from Jesus's command to love one's enemies, and from Gandhi, whose methods he studied in seminary and in India. In April 1963, jailed in Birmingham, he answered eight white Alabama clergymen who had called the protests unwise and untimely. In his *Letter from Birmingham Jail* he argued that a just law agrees with the moral law and that people have a moral duty to disobey unjust laws, openly and accepting the penalty.

King brought the movement north. In 1966 he rented an apartment in North Lawndale on Chicago's West Side and led marches against housing segregation. In Marquette Park a thrown rock struck him in the head. He said he had never seen hostility as fierce as he found in Chicago. King received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964, and he was assassinated in Memphis on April 4, 1968. The movement included many faiths, and also people of none. Jewish leaders such as Heschel marched with him, and so did Catholic nuns and Protestant ministers, while many white churches opposed him.

words.d: the struggle, strongest in the 1950s and 1960s, to end segregation and secure equal rights for Black Americans
King's term for a just society in which former enemies are reconciled and every person's dignity is honored
King's 1963 letter answering white clergymen, arguing for nonviolent disobedience of unjust laws
openly breaking a law one believes is unjust and accepting the penalty, in order to change it

look.prompt: King often quoted this verse in a modern translation: let justice roll down like waters. Why would a prophet's words written about ancient Israel speak to a movement in twentieth-century America?

lessons.title: Truth, Reconciliation and Interfaith Peacemakers
lessons.mainIdea: Desmond Tutu in South Africa and interfaith movements such as Liberia's women's peace campaign drew on religious teaching to end violence and heal societies.
reading: From 1948 South Africa's government enforced *apartheid*, a system of racial segregation that denied Black South Africans the vote and forced millions from their homes. Some white churches defended it. Others, and most Black churches, opposed it. Desmond Tutu, an Anglican priest, became a leading voice against it. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984, and in 1986 he became the first Black Archbishop of Cape Town. When apartheid ended and Nelson Mandela was elected president in 1994, the new government asked Tutu to chair the *Truth and Reconciliation Commission*.

The commission, which began hearings in 1996, invited victims to tell what had happened to them in public. It offered amnesty to people who confessed political crimes fully. Tutu often wept at the hearings. He explained the work through *ubuntu*, a southern African idea he summed up as a person is a person through other persons: my humanity is bound up with yours. He also spoke of Christian forgiveness, which he said was not forgetting and not excusing evil. Critics, including some victims' families, felt that amnesty let the guilty go free and that too little was paid in reparation. The commission became a model and a debate for other countries emerging from violence.

In Liberia in 2003, after years of civil war, Christian and Muslim women began to pray together in public. Led by Leymah Gbowee, a Lutheran social worker, and working with Muslim women's groups, they dressed in white and sat day after day by a fish market in Monrovia, demanding peace. They followed the peace talks to Ghana and blocked the doors until the negotiators reached an agreement. Gbowee shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2011. Such *interfaith* work, people of different faiths acting together from their own traditions, has become a recognized part of peacemaking around the world.

words.d: the system of legal racial segregation enforced in South Africa from 1948 until the early 1990s
the South African body, chaired by Desmond Tutu, that heard testimony about apartheid-era crimes from 1996
a southern African idea that a person becomes fully human through relationships with others
an official pardon for crimes, offered in South Africa to those who confessed political crimes fully
involving people of different religions working or speaking together, each from their own tradition

look.text: Hatred is never ended by hatred in this world. It is ended only by the absence of hatred, by love. This is an ancient and lasting law.

check.why: The commission offered amnesty in exchange for full confession, which some victims' families criticized.

Each tribe should govern itself

check.why: Tutu described ubuntu as the idea that one's humanity is bound up with the humanity of others.

check.q: What made the Liberian women's peace campaign of 2003 interfaith?

sections.title: Religious Freedom in the United States

lessons.title: Two Clauses, One Freedom
lessons.mainIdea: The First Amendment protects religious freedom in two ways: the Establishment Clause keeps government from sponsoring religion, and the Free Exercise Clause keeps it from restricting religion.
reading: Many colonies had official churches. Massachusetts taxed residents to support Congregational churches, and Virginia jailed Baptist preachers who preached without a license. Roger Williams, banished from Massachusetts, founded Rhode Island in 1636 on the principle of liberty of conscience. In 1786 Virginia passed the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, drafted by Thomas Jefferson and pushed through by James Madison. It declared that no one could be forced to attend or support any church. Baptists, Presbyterians and other minority churches were among its strongest supporters, because they had felt the weight of an official church themselves.

The First Amendment, ratified in 1791, begins with two clauses about religion. The *Establishment Clause* says Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion. The *Free Exercise Clause* says it shall not prohibit the free exercise of religion. The first keeps government from sponsoring, funding or favoring a faith. The second keeps it from punishing or burdening people for practicing one. In an 1802 letter to the Baptists of Danbury, Connecticut, Jefferson described the First Amendment as building a wall of separation between church and state. Courts and citizens still argue about how high and how solid that wall should be.

At first the First Amendment limited only the federal government. After the Fourteenth Amendment of 1868, the Supreme Court applied it to the states as well, the Free Exercise Clause in 1940 and the Establishment Clause in 1947. The two clauses can pull against each other. If a state pays for school buses to religious schools, is that establishment, or fair treatment of religious families? Judges on the Court have answered differently over the decades. Americans of every faith, and of none, have taken such questions to court.

words.d: the part of the First Amendment that forbids government to establish, sponsor or favor a religion
the part of the First Amendment that forbids government to prohibit the practice of religion
the freedom to hold and follow one's own beliefs about religion without being forced by the state
the principle, from Jefferson's 1802 phrase a wall of separation, that government and religious bodies stay independent

look.title: Which Clause Applies?
look.text: Case A: a city pays a pastor to lead prayers at the start of every public school day. Case B: a state fines a Sikh student for wearing a turban in a school photo. Case C: a town refuses a permit for a mosque while granting permits for churches of the same size. Case D: a state gives every private school, religious or not, the same textbook grant.

lessons.title: Free Exercise in the Courts
lessons.mainIdea: Supreme Court cases brought by Jehovah's Witnesses, the Amish, Native Americans and others have shaped how far government must make room for religious practice.
reading: In 1940 many public schools required students to salute the flag and recite the Pledge of Allegiance. Jehovah's Witnesses refused, because they believe saluting a flag breaks the commandment against bowing to images. Their children were expelled, and some Witness families were attacked. In 1943, in West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, the Supreme Court ruled that no official can force citizens to profess a belief. Justice Robert Jackson wrote that no official can prescribe what shall be orthodox in politics, religion or other matters of opinion. Jehovah's Witnesses brought dozens of cases in those years, and many of them expanded freedoms for everyone.

In 1972, in Wisconsin v. Yoder, the Court sided with Amish parents who would not send their children to school past the eighth grade. The Amish teach separation from worldly life, and the Court held that the state's interest did not outweigh their faith. But in 1990, in Employment Division v. Smith, the Court ruled against two members of the Native American Church. They had been fired and denied unemployment pay for using *peyote*, a cactus eaten as a sacrament in their ceremonies. The Court held that a law that applies to everyone and does not target religion can be enforced even if it burdens a religious practice.

The Smith ruling alarmed religious groups across the spectrum. In 1993 Congress passed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, or *RFRA*, almost unanimously. It requires the federal government to show a compelling reason before it substantially burdens someone's religious practice. In 1994 Congress also protected the sacramental use of peyote by members of Native American tribes. Later cases have used these laws and a related 2000 law covering prisons. In 2015 the Court ruled that an Arkansas prison had to let a Muslim prisoner grow a short beard. The pattern is steady: minority faiths, whose practices a majority may overlook, bring most free-exercise cases.

words.d: a Christian-rooted movement whose many court cases in the 1930s and 1940s expanded religious freedom in the United States
a Christian community in the Anabaptist tradition that lives separately from modern worldly life
a small cactus eaten as a sacrament in the ceremonies of the Native American Church
the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993, which requires the federal government to justify burdens on religious practice

lessons.title: Teaching About Religion in Public Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Public schools may not lead or sponsor worship, but they may teach about religion, and students keep the right to practice their own faith.
reading: Until the 1960s many public schools opened the day with a prayer or a Bible reading. In Engel v. Vitale in 1962 the Supreme Court ruled that a prayer written by New York state officials for students to recite broke the Establishment Clause. The next year, in Abington School District v. Schempp, it ruled the same about required daily Bible reading. The families who sued in the two cases included Jews, Unitarians and nonbelievers. The Court did not forbid the Bible in school. Justice Tom Clark wrote that a person's education is not complete without studying comparative religion and the history of religion, and that the Bible may be studied for its literary and historic qualities.

That distinction is the rule this course follows. Scholars sum it up this way: a public school may teach about religion but may not practice or promote it. Teaching about religion, the *academic study of religion*, describes what adherents believe and do, attributes every claim, and treats all traditions fairly. *Devotional* teaching aims to bring students to faith, and that belongs to families and religious communities. A lesson that says Muslims fast in Ramadan is academic. A teacher leading students in prayer is devotional, and in a public school that crosses the line.

Students have religious rights too. A student may pray alone or with friends, say grace before lunch, read a sacred text during free time, and write about faith in an assignment if it fits the topic. Under the *Equal Access Act* of 1984, if a public high school allows student clubs that are not about classes, it must allow religious clubs on the same terms. Students may wear religious clothing, such as a hijab, a kippah, a turban or a cross, with room made for their practice. In 2022, in Kennedy v. Bremerton, the Supreme Court ruled that a football coach's brief, quiet prayer at midfield after games was protected private speech, a decision that has been debated since.

words.d: describing and comparing religious beliefs and practices fairly, without promoting or opposing any of them
aimed at worship or at bringing people to faith; forbidden to public school staff as part of teaching
a 1984 law requiring public high schools that allow noncurricular clubs to allow religious clubs on the same terms
prayer led or sponsored by a public school, ruled unconstitutional in 1962; private student prayer remains protected

lessons.title: Persecution in Our Time
lessons.mainIdea: Religious persecution continues today against many communities, and international law names freedom of religion as a human right.
reading: After the Second World War and the Holocaust, the United Nations adopted the *Universal Declaration of Human Rights* in 1948. Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the committee that drafted it, and its members came from many faiths and none. Article 18 protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including the freedom to change one's religion. The declaration is not a treaty, but later treaties and many national constitutions built on it. Religious freedom in this sense covers believers of every kind and people who hold no religion.

*Persecution* means harming people because of who they are or what they believe. It continues today, and researchers track it. In August 2014 the militant group that called itself the Islamic State attacked the *Yazidis*, a religious minority in northern Iraq, killing thousands of men and enslaving women and girls; a UN commission called it genocide. In 2017 more than 700,000 *Rohingya*, a mostly Muslim people, fled Myanmar's army into Bangladesh. In China's Xinjiang region, a 2022 UN human rights report described the detention of large numbers of Uyghur and other Muslims as possible crimes against humanity; China's government rejects that account. In Iran members of the Bahá'í faith have long been barred from universities.

Persecution falls on many groups, including Christians in several countries, Ahmadi Muslims in Pakistan, Jews facing antisemitism and Muslims facing anti-Muslim hatred in Europe and the United States, and people who leave religion in countries that punish it. Sometimes governments do it, and sometimes armed groups or mobs do. Researchers such as the Pew Research Center measure both government restrictions and hostility from society. Scholars caution that the same group can be a majority that persecutes in one country and a minority that suffers in another. Describing persecution accurately means naming the victims, the perpetrators, the place and the date.

words.d: the 1948 United Nations statement of basic rights; Article 18 protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion
harming people, through violence, law or discrimination, because of their identity or beliefs
a religious minority of northern Iraq with their own ancient faith, attacked by the Islamic State group in 2014

lessons.title: Chicago's Parliament and Interfaith City
lessons.mainIdea: The 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago began the modern interfaith movement, and the city remains a center of interfaith life.
reading: In September 1893, while the World's Columbian Exposition filled Chicago's South Side, the *World's Parliament of Religions* met downtown from September 11 to 27, in the new building that now houses the Art Institute of Chicago. It was the first formal gathering of representatives of the world's religions in the West. Most speakers were Protestant Christians, and its organizers hoped Christianity would be seen at its best. But the speakers who drew the most attention came from Asia. Swami Vivekananda, a Hindu monk from Bengal, opened his first speech with the words Sisters and Brothers of America and was greeted with a long ovation.

Other voices made history too. Anagarika Dharmapala of Sri Lanka spoke for Theravada Buddhism, and Soyen Shaku, a Japanese Zen master, came from Kamakura. Virchand Gandhi presented Jainism, and Mohammed Alexander Russell Webb, an American convert, spoke about Islam. Jewish rabbis and Catholic bishops took part, and so did women speakers. The Parliament also had limits. Some groups were left out, and Native American religions were not presented by their own practitioners. Still, historians date the American interest in Hinduism and Buddhism, and the modern *interfaith movement*, to that September in Chicago.

In 1993 Chicago hosted a centennial Parliament, where thousands gathered and many leaders endorsed a statement called Towards a Global Ethic. The Parliament has since met in cities such as Cape Town, Barcelona, Melbourne, Salt Lake City and Toronto, and it returned to Chicago in 2023. The Chicago area is one of the most religiously diverse places in the country. It has the Bahá'í House of Worship in Wilmette, Hindu temples in the suburbs, the Buddhist Temple of Chicago in Uptown, and large mosques in the southwest suburbs. KAM Isaiah Israel continues the oldest Jewish congregation in the city, founded in 1847. Interfaith councils and student groups bring these communities together to serve and to learn.

words.d: the 1893 gathering in Chicago of representatives of many religions, the first of its kind in the West
a Hindu monk from Bengal whose speeches at the 1893 Parliament drew wide American interest in Hinduism
organized efforts for people of different religions to meet, understand one another and work together
the hundredth anniversary of an event; Chicago hosted the Parliament's centennial in 1993
